finding.claim: isInSubnet/isHostInSubnet compare only bit prefixes and never check address family, so an Address4 can be reported as inside an Address6 range (and vice versa) when the leading bits coincide.
finding.source: Any caller-supplied IP string parsed by new Address4(...) or new Address6(...), e.g. from X-Forwarded-For or a request body.
finding.sink: Public containment check isInSubnet (ipv4.ts:455, ipv6.ts:1216 -> common.ts:19-25) used as an allow/deny gate against mixed-family CIDR lists.

trace.note: isInSubnet is bound to common.isInSubnet for Address4
isInSubnet(this: Address4|Address6, address: Address4|Address6) accepts either family
only check is this.subnetMask < address.subnetMask
delegates to isHostInSubnet
returns this.mask(address.subnetMask) === address.mask(); v4 bits and v6 bits are compared directly, no family check

finding.guards_checked: Subnet-ordering check (common.ts:20) only. No family/type check in isInSubnet, isHostInSubnet, or their callers. Built-in classifiers (isPrivate, isLoopback, getType, etc.) only use same-family ranges, so they are not affected. Repro by reading: new Address4('252.1.2.3').isInSubnet(new Address6('fc00::/7')) -> 32>=7, mask(7) of 252 is '1111110' which equals fc00::/7 mask -> true; new Address4('32.0.0.1').isInSubnet(new Address6('2000::/3')) -> true.

finding.claim: The IPv6 zone identifier is extracted and stored in .zone without any validation, and isValid() returns true for an address with arbitrary zone text.
finding.source: Caller-supplied string passed to new Address6(...) / Address6.isValid(...), e.g. '::1%<anything>'.
finding.sink: Address6.zone property (ipv6.ts:110), consumed by callers who rebuild a scoped address for a socket, command, or URL; isValid gate at ipv6.ts:167-176.

trace.note: RE_ZONE_STRING.exec(address) on the full remaining string
RE_ZONE_STRING = /%.*$/ matches everything from the first % to end, with no character-class restriction
this.zone = zone[0] stores raw text, including '%'
address stripped of zone before parse, so RE_BAD_CHARACTERS (constants.ts:61) never sees the zone
isValid returns true when the prefix parses

finding.guards_checked: Newline in zone is rejected indirectly (regex fails, then RE_BAD_CHARACTERS sees the newline). Other special characters (space, quote, semicolon, <, >) pass. Library outputs correctForm, href, link, group, and HTML helpers all exclude the zone (ipv6.ts:665, 1451, 1469, 1514), so exposure only happens when a consumer reads .zone. Repro by reading: Address6.isValid('::1%x" onmouseover=alert(1) "') -> true; new Address6('fe80::1%a b').zone === '%a b'.

finding.claim: embeddedIPv4() only unwraps IPv4-mapped and NAT64 well-known addresses, so isPrivate/isLoopback/isLinkLocal/isUnspecified/isCGNAT/isBroadcast/isMulticast do not classify IPv4 addresses embedded in 6to4 (2002::/16) or Teredo (2001::/32) addresses.
finding.source: Attacker-supplied IPv6 literal such as 2002:0a00:0001:: (embeds 10.0.0.1) or 2002:7f00:0001:: (embeds 127.0.0.1).
finding.sink: Trust-boundary classifiers (isPrivate, isLoopback) that the library's own docs recommend for SSRF allow/deny filters.

trace.note: embeddedIPv4 checks only isMapped4() or NAT64_WELL_KNOWN_SUBNET
isPrivate: embedded is null, so falls through to isULA (fc00::/7) and NAT64 local-use only
isLoopback: embedded is null, so returns getType()==='Loopback', which is false
2002::/16 is typed as '6to4' and never unwrapped

finding.guards_checked: Documented scope: embeddedIPv4 doc (ipv6.ts:1300-1316) explicitly names only mapped and NAT64 well-known. is6to4()/inspect6to4() exist but are not used by the classifiers. Exploitation needs the target to route 6to4 or Teredo to the embedded IPv4, which usually depends on a relay the attacker does not control, so impact is limited.

finding.claim: RE_ZONE_STRING /%.*$/ is quadratic on crafted input: each '%' scans to the next line terminator and then backtracks, so a long string of '%' followed by a newline costs O(n^2) inside the Address6 constructor.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled string of length n passed to new Address6(...) or Address6.isValid(...), e.g. a large JSON field or query value, containing many '%' and a '\n' before end of input.
finding.sink: RE_ZONE_STRING.exec in the Address6 constructor, which runs before any format validation.

trace.note: constructor accepts the raw string with no length cap
RE_SUBNET_STRING.exec runs first (linear)
/\// test runs next (linear)
RE_ZONE_STRING.exec on the full string
%.* stops at \n and $ cannot match there (no m flag), so each % start backtracks over the rest of the line: O(k*n)

finding.guards_checked: No input length limit in the constructor or isValid. Regexes elsewhere are anchored and linear (RE_URL, RE_ADDRESS, RE_BAD_CHARACTERS, RE_BAD_ADDRESS). Not executed: this is from reading the regex semantics, with no runtime tool available to measure it.

finding.claim: Address6.fromWildcard accepts the malformed pattern ':::' and silently returns the valid address '::/128' instead of throwing.
finding.source: Wildcard pattern string, from configuration or other input the caller treats as an allowlist/ACL spec.
finding.sink: Returned Address6 used as an ACL or range boundary.

trace.note: left = [] because halves[0] === ''
remaining = 8 - 0 - 2 = 6, so only the remaining>=1 check passes
group count is 8, so the length check passes
builds '0:0:0:0:0:0::/128', which the constructor parses as '::'

finding.guards_checked: Rejects '%' and '/', more than one '::', too many groups, and interior wildcards. Does not reject empty groups produced by a ':::' run. Severity depends on whether the pattern can come from untrusted input or only from misconfiguration.

finding.claim: Address6.fromURL returns { address: null } for URLs that contain userinfo (for example http://user@[::1]/). Callers that guard with 'if (address && ...)' skip the check and fail open.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled URL string passed to Address6.fromURL, e.g. http://user@[::1]/.
finding.sink: Caller's allow/deny decision using the returned address, followed by a native fetch of the same URL (which resolves to ::1).

trace.note: protocol prefix stripped, leaving 'user@[::1]/'
'[' present but no ']:', so takes the bare-host branch
RE_URL.exec on 'user@[::1]/' fails: 'u' is not in [0-9a-f:.] and the next char after the host must be [/?#]
returns { error, address: null, port: null }
RE_URL is anchored, so the regex correctly rejects the userinfo form

finding.guards_checked: Library fails closed (no wrong address returned), and the regex is anchored. Risk is the caller ignoring result.error. Informational API footgun, not a library bypass.
